label: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017
output:
# My Van Almost Caught Fire. Here's What Went Wrong.

On October 28th, a little after 2pm, I was in a client's driveway in Bedford with a wet Bernese mountain dog and a van that was quietly trying to burn itself down.

I want to be upfront about something before I get into this: I am not an electrician. I'm a mobile dog groomer. Everything technical in this post came from Priya at Sackville Marine Electric, who is an electrician, and from the paperwork that came with my gear. She explained it to me twice, once with a calculator and once with a drawing on the back of a quote. If something in your van worries you, get a professional to look at it. Please don't take my word for the fine details. Take my word for the fact that this stuff matters.

## What happened

Moose was on the table. If you've done a Bernese you know they're roughly the size of a small sofa and they take a while. I had him on high, working through the back end, and I kept getting this smell of hot plastic. I figured it was the dryer motor. Dryers get hot, they smell weird, it happens. I kept going for longer than I should have.

Then I looked up and saw smoke coming out from under the bench seat where the batteries live.

Not a lot. But smoke. Actual smoke, in a wooden box, in a van, next to a dog.

I killed the battery switch. I got Moose out the side door, still damp, and he was thrilled honestly, he thought it was the best day of his life. I hit it with the extinguisher because I didn't know what else to do, and I'm still not sure I needed to. When I finally got a look, the lug on the positive end was black, and the jacket on the cable had melted back about 3cm.

Moose's mom brought me a coffee and sat with me on her steps while I shook.

Everyone's fine. Moose is fine. The van is not fine. I'm off the road for weeks and I'm slowly losing my mind, but I'll get to that.

## What actually went wrong

Here's the setup in my van, which was built in spring 2025 by Coastline Van Fitouts, Darren's outfit:

- 3000W inverter
- two 200Ah lithium batteries, 12V
- cable from battery to inverter: 4 AWG

Priya took one look and said that cable should have been 2/0 for a 3000W inverter on a 12V system. (That's "two-ought." I had to ask.)

The reason is arithmetic, and it's the kind of arithmetic I wish I'd done before I paid anybody.

A 3000W inverter on a 12V system pulls 3000 ÷ 12 = 250 amps. That's at full load, before you account for the fact that the inverter itself wastes some energy as heat, so realistically it's a bit more than that. My dryer on high pulls around 1800–2000W, which is 150–167 amps at 12V. Add the water heater if it kicks in at the same time and you're up around 200–250 amps running through one cable, which is the entire point of the cable.

4 AWG copper is rated for somewhere in the ballpark of 60 to 100 amps in a real-world install, depending on the insulation and how it's bundled and whether it's sitting in a hot compartment. Even the generous numbers don't get within a hundred amps of what my dryer was asking for. I was running two to three times the rated capacity of that cable, over and over, every groom.

So that's problem one. The cable was too small, and not by a little.

## Problem two was worse

The lug on the positive end, the metal fitting that clamps onto the end of the cable so it can bolt to the battery or the inverter, had been crimped with pliers or a hammer. Not a proper crimper. And the heat-shrink was covering it, so it looked completely normal from the outside. Tidy.

Priya explained this part to me with a calculator, and it's the bit that has kept me up.

A bad crimp is a bad connection, and a bad connection is resistance. Resistance turns current into heat. If a connection has a resistance of just a hundredth of an ohm, and you push 200 amps through it, you're dropping two volts across it and generating about 400 watts of heat in a space the size of your thumb.

Four hundred watts. That's a soldering iron. That's a small appliance heating element, buried under heat-shrink, inside a wooden bench seat, sitting next to two lithium batteries.

You can have a perfectly sized cable and still cook it at the lug. I had both things wrong at once. The cable was undersized, which meant it was running hot anyway, and then the connection on the end was adding its own heat on top of that.

That's why the smell came before the smoke, and it's why I thought it was the dryer. It genuinely was hot plastic. I just had the wrong appliance.

## The fuse was never going to save me

My build had a 300A ANL fuse on the main run.

A fuse has one job: protect the cable. Not the inverter, not the batteries, the cable. It's there so that if something goes badly wrong, the fuse dies before the wire does.

A 4 AWG cable should have been fused somewhere around 100–150A. Mine had a 300A fuse on it, which means that fuse would have cheerfully let 290 amps cook that cable all afternoon without ever blowing. It was sized for the inverter's appetite, not the cable's capacity. Which is backwards.

This is the part I want every groomer reading this to understand, because it's the cheapest thing to check and the most likely thing to be wrong: **if your cable melted but your fuse is still intact, your fuse was never sized to protect your cable.** That's not bad luck. That's a design problem.

The second issue with the fuse was where it was. Mine was mounted about 90cm from the battery. Priya said it should be within roughly 18cm. The reason is that the cable between the battery and the fuse is live all the time, with no protection at all. If 90cm of unprotected cable chafes through on a seat frame or a metal edge somewhere, that's a dead short with nothing to stop it except the battery's own willingness to give up everything it has.

She also would have used a Class T fuse instead of an ANL. ANL fuses can't reliably interrupt the amount of current a big lithium bank can dump into a dead short. I'm not going to pretend I fully understand the engineering there, but her summary was that a 400Ah lithium bank can dump thousands of amps in a fraction of a second, and the fuse has to be able to slam the door on that. A Class T is built for it. The ANL isn't.

## The comparison that made me feel sick

Priya pulled up my damage photos next to thermal camera images of her own van, running a comparable load through its inverter. Hers barely gets warm. A few degrees above ambient at the lugs, and that's it.

Mine had been cooking itself for months. I'd been climbing in and out of that van every day, drying dogs, running the water heater, and the whole time there was a 400-watt heater buried in the bench seat.

She asked me if I'd ever noticed the bench feeling warm. And honestly, yeah. I thought it was the batteries doing their thing. I thought warm was normal. Nobody had ever told me what normal looked like.

## What this is costing

The repair quote is $4,200. That covers rewiring the main runs, a new fuse block, and a Class T fuse. Three weeks minimum, and some of the parts are on order.

I've cancelled 31 appointments so far. Insurance says maybe. The adjuster is coming Thursday, and I have no idea what that conversation is going to look like.

Rent is due on the 1st and my entire income is that van. I'm not going to dress that up. I'm scared, and I'm bored, and I'm not sleeping great, and there's a version of this where I'm writing a very different post about a dog in a burning van. I keep thinking about that version.

## Tasha, this part is for you

You're about to put a deposit down with the same builder. I'm not writing this to trash Darren publicly. He hasn't answered three texts and an email, which tells you something, but the rest of it I'll just state as facts and you can decide what to do with them.

Before you pay anything, get these in writing. Not in a text, not in a conversation at the van, in writing, on the quote or in an email you keep:

- **The cable size for every main run.** Battery to inverter, battery to fuse block, fuse block to everything else. In AWG. Written down.
- **The fuse type, rating, and location.** Specifically how far the fuse sits from the battery, in centimetres.
- **How the lugs are crimped.** Proper crimper, hydraulic press, or factory-made cables. Not pliers. Ask them to say it.
- **Whether the inverter manufacturer's spec was followed**, and what that spec says. Your inverter manual will list a recommended cable size and fuse rating. Ask them to compare their plan to the manual, in front of you.
- **Photos of the crimps before the heat-shrink goes on.** This is the single easiest ask and it costs them nothing if they're doing it right. If they won't, that's your answer.
- **A wiring diagram** you can keep.
- **Who is physically doing the electrical work**, and what their background is.
- **At least one other van they've done** that you can look at, ideally one that's been in service a year.

And here's the thing I'd say to anybody, not just you: **tidy is not the same as right.** My build looked beautiful. The cables were loomed, the heat-shrink was neat, the bench was finished. None of that told me whether the crimp was good or whether the fuse was the right size, and I didn't know enough to ask. You don't have to know enough to ask. You just have to make them write it down.

## The checklist

This is the part I most wanted to write, because when this happened I went looking for something practical and everything I found was either a forum argument or a 40-page marine electrical standard.

You can do all of this on your own van with the power off. Take your jewelry off, don't wave any tools around near the battery terminals, and don't undo a single bolt. This is a look-and-see list, not a repair list. If you find something, take photos and call somebody.

**1. Find your inverter cables and read the jacket.** There's usually a printed gauge on the cable itself. If you can't find it, compare the copper thickness to a known cable, or ask. Write the number down and compare it to your inverter manual's recommendation.

**2. Look at every lug with a light.** You're looking for three things: plier marks or hammer marks, discoloration (brown, black, or a crusty green), and stiff or hardened insulation near the terminal. If a lug is covered in heat-shrink, that's fine, but run your finger along the cable just past it and feel for stiffness or a lumpy, uneven shape underneath.

**3. Find your fuse. Measure how far it is from the battery.** If it's more than about 18cm, ask your builder why. Note the rating and the type. Then compare the rating to what your cable is actually rated for. A big fuse on a small cable is decoration.

**4. Check where cables pass through anything metal.** Look for grommets, split loom, or a protective sleeve. Any metal edge touching a cable is a future short. Also check that cables are secured and not flopping around or resting on something sharp.

**5. Look at your battery terminals.** Any white or green crust, any blackening, any signs of heat discoloration. Check that the terminal bolts are snug, not gorilla-tight. Don't go reefing on them.

**6. Check you have a smoke detector in the back.** Mine only had the one that came with the van, in the cab. Six feet away from the batteries, behind a bulkhead. That's not where the smoke is going to be. A basic battery-powered smoke detector is fifteen or twenty bucks and it's the best money you'll spend on that van.

**7. Check your extinguisher.** Is it actually in the van, is it charged, is it somewhere you can reach it in five seconds from the driver's seat? Mine was buried under a bag of towels. I got lucky.

**8. Know what your loads are.** Add up the actual wattage of your dryer, your water heater, and anything else that runs at the same time. If that total, divided by 12, is anywhere near the capacity of your inverter or your cable, you have a conversation to have with a professional. My dryer alone was 2000W. Nobody ever asked me what my dryer drew. I didn't know to tell them.

**9. If you want to be extra, buy a cheap infrared thermometer.** I got mine at Canadian Tire for $40 after this happened, which is closing the barn door after the horse has set fire to the barn, but you can do it before. Run your dryer for ten minutes under load, then point it at every lug and every cable end. Compare the readings to the ambient temperature in the van and to each other. If one lug is dramatically hotter than the others, or if anything is more than warm to the touch, stop using it and get it looked at. Priya's thermal photos showed me what "normal" looks like. Normal is boring. Normal is barely above room temperature. Warm is not normal.

**10. Take photos of everything now.** Before anything happens, while the van is fine, so you have a baseline and so you have evidence if you ever need it for insurance. I wish I'd done this. I've been scrolling through my camera roll trying to find pictures of the build from a year ago.

## The lesson I keep coming back to

I trusted the build because it looked tidy. That's the whole thing, really. I don't have the background to evaluate a crimp, so I evaluated what I could see, which was neat loom and clean cabinetry and a bench that looked like furniture. Tidy is not a safety standard. Tidy is not a test.

The other thing is that this failed slowly and then quickly. It didn't happen because I did something wrong on October 28th. It happened because that cable and that lug had been getting hotter every single time I turned the dryer on, for months, and nothing anywhere in that van told me so. There was no alarm, no warning, no gauge. Just a smell I misread.

## Where I'm at

The van goes in when the parts arrive. Three weeks, minimum, and I'm trying not to think about what happens if it's four. The adjuster comes Thursday. Darren still hasn't called back. I've got a list of clients who've been lovely about it and a list of clients I've had to let down and I'm trying to focus on the first list.

I'll be honest, some days I sit in my kitchen and think about the fact that the entire thing, my house, my food, my rent, is a 12V system and a crimp I never looked at. That's not a fun thought to have at 3am.

But the plan is to come back with a van that's wired properly, with a Class T fuse and a smoke detector and a thermal thermometer in the door pocket, and to be annoyingly vocal about all of it for the rest of my career.

I'll post again when the van's back and I've got Moose on a table. Give your dogs a scratch for me, and go look at your lugs.

— if you've got questions about your own build, comment or message me and I'll pass them to Priya, who has been extremely patient with me and deserves a coffee.
